opus-5.5.text:
That's a good question, and honestly, I think about it quite a lot. One habit I really need to change is my tendency to want to do everything myself. When I was working on Taichi, especially in the early days during my PhD, I wrote most of the code myself, and that worked because the project was small and I knew every corner of it. But as the project grew and later as we started a company, that habit became a bottleneck. I'd find myself thinking, "It's faster if I just fix this myself," instead of taking the time to explain the context to someone else and let them own it. In the short term, that's true, it is faster. In the long term, it's terrible, because the team doesn't grow and I become the single point of failure.

Related to that, I'm something of a perfectionist when it comes to engineering details. I care a lot about whether an API feels elegant, whether the compiler design is clean. That's useful when you're building a programming language, because users really feel those details. But sometimes I spend too much time polishing things that don't matter much yet, when what we actually need is to ship something, get feedback, and iterate. I've had to learn to distinguish between decisions that are hard to reverse, where it's worth being careful, and decisions that are easy to change later, where you should just move fast.

The third thing is balance. For a long time I treated work as almost the only thing, coding late into the night, thinking about problems constantly. Some of that passion is genuinely what drives me, and I don't want to lose it. But I've realized that sustainable productivity matters more than bursts of intensity. If you burn yourself out, you can't think clearly, and in research and engineering, clear thinking is everything. So I'm trying to be more deliberate about rest, exercise, and stepping back to think about direction rather than just grinding on execution.

So in summary: delegate more, be pragmatic about perfection, and work in a way I can sustain for decades, not just months.

r001.rationale: He says he needs to step back and think about direction instead of “just grinding on execution,” clearly identifying an execution-heavy habit to change.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good question, and honestly one I ask myself a lot.

The biggest one is probably my tendency to want to do everything myself. When I was working on Taichi as a PhD student, that was fine, even necessary. I wrote the compiler, I wrote the docs, I answered the GitHub issues at two in the morning. But once you're running a company, that habit becomes a liability. Every hour I spend fixing a bug that someone on the team could fix is an hour I'm not spending on the things only I can do, like thinking about where the product should be in two years, or talking to users. I know this intellectually, but the pull of "I could just fix this in twenty minutes" is very strong. Engineers will understand what I mean.

The second one is related. I tend to optimize for being right rather than for being clear. In research, correctness is the whole game. In a company, you can be completely correct and still fail because nobody understood what you were asking for, or because you convinced yourself instead of convincing the team. I've had to learn that explaining the "why" three times is not wasted effort. It's actually the job.

And the third thing, which is a bit more personal, is that I've historically treated rest as something you earn after the work is done. The problem is the work is never done. There's no moment where the backlog is empty and you get to relax. So I've been trying to treat recovery as part of the process rather than a reward for finishing it. I'm not great at it yet. But I've noticed that the ideas I'm most proud of almost never came while I was grinding. They came while walking, or in the shower, or talking to someone about something unrelated. So there's a very practical argument for it, not just a wellness one.

If I had to summarize, I'd say: delegate more, explain more, and stop more. Simple to say, hard to do.

r001.rationale: He says he needs to stop doing everything himself and describes spending time fixing bugs instead of thinking about the product’s future or talking to users.

astra-6.text: I think I need to get better at prioritizing. When I see an interesting technical problem, I tend to dive into it and spend a lot of time trying to find an elegant solution. But the most interesting problem isn’t always the most important one. I’d like to pause more often and ask, “Does this actually need to be solved right now?” And I need to get better at delegating—giving other people room to solve things in their own way instead of feeling that I should work through every detail myself.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he spends too much time pursuing technical problems and needs to prioritize, but does not identify spending more time executing than thinking.

sol-6.1.text: I think I need to get better at delegating. My instinct is often to dive into a technical problem and solve it myself, because I enjoy that process. But when you’re working with a team, that can become a bottleneck. I need to spend more time explaining the goal, giving people enough context, and then trusting them to find their own solution. It also means being more deliberate about what really needs my attention, instead of treating every interesting problem as something I should work on.
